Invasion
in-VAY-zhun
n. (a hostile entry into another's territory)
From Latin invadere, to go in upon. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the mouth of an Egyptian servant left for dead by the Amalekites, reporting the raid that had burned Ziklag.

Biblical Definition

We made an invasion upon the south of the Cherethites, and upon the coast which belongeth to Judah, and upon the south of Caleb; and we burned Ziklag with fire. The speaker is a sick Egyptian slave abandoned in a field, whom David's men fed with bread and figs and raisins before he would talk. David had come home to find Ziklag burned and every wife and child taken, and his own men speaking of stoning him. What the chapter is known for is the verse in the middle of that: David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God. Then he did the thing he always did at his best — David enquired at the LORD, saying, Shall I pursue after this troop? And the answer came with the outcome attached: Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all. And he did: David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away. He also settled the law of the spoil that day, that as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a hostile entrance into the possessions of another; particularly, the entrance of a hostile army into a country for the purpose of conquest.

expand to see more

INVASION, n. A hostile entrance into the possessions of another; particularly, the entrance of a hostile army.

INROAD, n. The entrance of an enemy into a country with purposes of hostility; a sudden or desultory incursion.

SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; plunder; pillage; booty.

DISTRESS, n. Extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; affliction; calamity.

ENQUIRE, v.i. To ask a question; in Scripture, to seek direction of the LORD.

Key Scripture

1Sa 30:14 — "We made an invasion upon the south of the Cherethites, and upon the coast which belongeth to Judah, and upon the south of Caleb; and we burned Ziklag with fire."

1Sa 30:6 — "And David was greatly distressed; for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters: but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God."

1Sa 30:8 — "And David enquired at the LORD, saying, Shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them? And he answered him, Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all."

1Sa 30:18 — "And David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away: and David rescued his two wives."

Modern Corruption

Encouragement is sought in circumstances, in a leader's own resolve, or in the support of his people; David's men were about to stone him and he encouraged himself in the LORD his God, then asked God what to do.

expand to see more

1 Samuel 30:6 is one of the most useful verses in Scripture for a man in leadership on his worst day, and the order of its clauses is the whole lesson. David was greatly distressed — the distress is granted, not denied. The people spake of stoning him — his support was gone. The soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and for his daughters — and their grief was legitimate, since David's own decisions had left Ziklag unguarded. There is no circumstance left to draw on and no innocence to appeal to. But David encouraged himself in the LORD his God, which is an act, not a feeling, and it is the only source left when everything else is burned.

What follows is the pattern the dictionary keeps. He did not act on the encouragement by charging out; he enquired at the LORD and waited for an answer, and the answer told him both to go and what would happen. Then, having recovered all, he refused to let two hundred exhausted men be cut out of the spoil by the sons of Belial among his own troops, and made it a statute in Israel that the man who keeps the baggage shares with the man in the line. Recovery, and then justice in the division of it, on the same day.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pashat (H6584), to strip off, to raid, to make an invasion; chazaq (H2388), to strengthen oneself; natsal (H5337), to deliver or recover.

expand to see more

Hebrew pashat (H6584) — to strip, to spread out, to make a raid; we made an invasion.

Hebrew gedud (H1416) — a band, a troop, a raiding party; shall I pursue after this troop.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to strengthen oneself; David encouraged himself in the LORD.

Hebrew sha'al (H7592) — to ask, to enquire; David enquired at the LORD.

Hebrew natsal (H5337) — to snatch away, to deliver, to recover; David recovered all.

Usage

"“We made an invasion upon the south of the Cherethites” — the single occurrence."

"“but David encouraged himself in the LORD his God” — the verse the chapter is known for."

"“Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them” — the answer to the enquiry."
